gates.title: Do lab-grown islet cells work as a treatment in people?
gates.plain: Yes, once they survive. In Vertex’s trial, all 12 people given the full dose reached their blood-sugar targets, and 10 of the 12 no longer needed insulin injections after a year. They all take anti-rejection drugs, which Islet-1 is designed to remove, and layering Islet-1’s extra gene edits on top still has to be checked in the lab so normal insulin and glucagon control holds.
gates.evidence: Vertex VX-880 (zimislecel). Reichman and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025.

gates.title: Does the genetic cloak stop rejection without anti-rejection drugs?
gates.plain: It has worked once: in one person, edited donor islet cells were left alone for more than a year with no anti-rejection drugs. Rather than bet all three blueprints on one identical cloak, Design A uses the standard HLA-E and CD47 cloak, Design B keeps one matched HLA-C gene checked against a 22-species foreign-peptide scan, and Design X screens a 20-variant HLA-E panel to avoid triggering activating NKG2C natural killer cells.
gates.evidence: Sana UP421. Carlsson and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025, plus Islet-1’s HLA-E and HLA-C sequence models (IIP-0016, IIP-0017).
gates.next: Next: test all three cloaks head to head on stem-cell islets (Stage 1, lab testing).

gates.title: Can the cells survive the autoimmune attack that caused the diabetes?
gates.plain: This is the hardest step. People with type 1 diabetes carry immune cells that remember beta cells, plus inflammatory signals (IL-1 and Fas ligand) that can kill nearby cells even when MHC flags are hidden. Design A pairs scar-free SERPINB9 with a transient Fas-ligand gel, Design B dampens interferon signalling via a protective TYK2 variant, and Design X dials down the cell’s own IL-1 and Fas death receptors.
gates.evidence: Anchored to the single human autoimmune graft follow-up (Sana UP421, above) and Islet-1’s receptor-shield and TYK2 models (IIP-0012, IIP-0017, IIP-0018).
gates.next: Next: head-to-head cytokine and T-cell stress tests (Stage 1, lab testing).

gates.title: Does the oxygen layer keep the graft alive until blood vessels grow in?
gates.plain: A new graft has no blood vessels at first. Explicit 3D physics simulations caught two hidden hazards—cell clusters clumping together and peroxide spikes next to oxygen-releasing beads—so Designs A and X add ordered microwells, wet-sieved beads of 50 µm or less and a catalase barrier film at least 20 µm thick, while Design B tests an independent 140 µm bead-free pre-vascularized sheet with no peroxide chemistry.
gates.evidence: From Islet-1’s 3D finite-volume oxygen and peroxide simulations (IIP-0019). None of these values has been measured in the lab yet.
gates.next: Next: microwell, peroxide-barrier and blood-vessel tests (Stage 2).
